standard.title: Paragraphs group information
standard.description: understand that paragraphs are a key organisational feature of the stages of written texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how cohesion devices including overviews and paragraph structure guide readers (AC9E2LA04 — implicitly). They have not yet examined how paragraphs function as the primary organisational unit that groups information into the stages of a text.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand that paragraphs are a key organisational feature — grouping related information and marking the stages of written texts.

nodes.label: Paragraphs in informative texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that paragraphs in informative texts group related information together, often beginning with a topic sentence.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two paragraphs in an informative text and explain what related information each groups together.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise that informative texts are organised into paragraphs beginning with a topic sentence, grouping related ideas; examine models of well-constructed paragraphs and identify their features.
wider: Examine how the topic sentences of successive paragraphs map the overall structure of an informative text — reading just the first sentences to get the main ideas
Compare two versions of the same information — one organised into paragraphs, one without — and discuss the effect on the reader
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who haven't established the informative paragraph model at N1 have no baseline rule to contrast with at N2 — the narrative paragraphing lesson depends on students first understanding (and potentially over-applying) the topic-sentence convention.

response_modes.reason: Students often see paragraph breaks as arbitrary or stylistic. Examining models across different informative text types — reports, explanations, recounts — helps students see that paragraph breaks always signal a shift in focus, regardless of text type.

success_criteria: Student identifies what information a paragraph groups together
Student explains why those pieces of information belong in the same paragraph (what makes them related)

nodes.label: Paragraphs in narrative texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise that paragraphs in narrative texts vary in length and serve different purposes — they do not always follow a predictable pattern formula.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify paragraphs in a narrative text and notice that they vary in length, explaining one example of why a short or long paragraph is used at a particular point.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise that narrative paragraphs vary in length and purpose — some build tension, some shift scene, some develop character — and do not always follow a topic-sentence pattern. Examine models of effective narrative paragraphing.
wider: Compare how a very short paragraph (even one sentence) is used for effect in a narrative versus a long descriptive paragraph — discuss what each achieves
Experiment with changing the paragraph breaks in a narrative extract and evaluate how it changes the reading experience

response_modes.reason: Students taught the topic-sentence rule may misapply it to narrative. Seeing that narrative paragraphing follows different logic — and that variation itself is a tool — prevents the misconception that all paragraphs work the same way.

success_criteria: Student identifies that narrative paragraphs vary in length
Student explains one example of why a paragraph starts or ends at a particular point in a narrative
